q: Shor's algorithm factoring an n-bit integer N runs in time O(n² log n log log n) on a quantum computer. The key quantum step uses the quantum Fourier transform to find the period r of the function f(x) = a^x mod N for random a. The classical reduction reduces factoring to:
opts: Finding the period r of f(x) = aˣ mod N: if r is even and a^{r/2} ≢ −1 mod N, then gcd(a^{r/2}±1, N) gives a non-trivial factor
Finding a prime factorisation of N−1
exp: Shor's classical reduction: pick random a, find period r of aˣ (mod N). If r is even and a^{r/2} ≢ ±1 (mod N), then gcd(a^{r/2}±1, N) is a non-trivial factor. The QFT finds r in O(n²) quantum gates, exponentially faster than classical period-finding (best known: sub-exponential).
